https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/20/ezek.text: Menü Kereső Ezek lesznek Magyar Péter új országjárásának helyszínei Belföld Vorák Anita Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Magyar Péter már májusban is beszélt arról , hogy a nyár végén újra országjárásra indul, majd a parlament június 1-i ülésén Pócs Jánosnak üzengetve azt is elárulta, hogy augusztus 20-án kezd. Még a fideszes képviselőt is invitálta. „Ha van kedve vagy van energiája, jöjjön el velem, augusztus 20-ától én újra elindulok egy országjárásra. Nem lesz egyszerű, mert néha hat-hét helyen fogunk megállni naponta, sokat kell beszélni, nem lesz TEK, nem lesz zárt csarnok.” Az elmúlt hetekben Magyar Péter a paksi munkára koncentrált, az országjárásról nem sok szó esett. Még a Tisza Szigetek országos találkozóján is majdnem elfejtett beszélni róla, de aztán a közös éneklés után elárulta, hogy merre indul. A következő településeket fogja végigjárni: Dunaújváros, Pécs, Kisvárda, Miskolc, Veszprém, Gyula, Szeged, Veresegyház, Kecskemét, Szolnok, Debrecen, Szombathely, Nagykanizsa, Esztergom, Székesfehérvár, és végül Budapest. Hogy egy nap hány helyszínre látogat el, azt nem mondta el, és azt sem, hogy pontosan mikor indul. Megkérdeztük erről a Tisza Pártot, ha válaszolnak, frissítjük a cikket. Magyar bejelentette, hogy augusztus végén a miniszterek is országjárásra indulnak, többek között Ruff Bálint, Kapitány István és Orbán Anita is. Magyar Péter utoljára a választások előtt, február 16-tól 56 napon át, április 12-ig járta az országot. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5ye.text: Image source, Reuters By Dan Sales Â and Â James Landale ,Â Diplomatic correspondent Published 4 September 2026, 16:55 BST Updated 4 hours ago A Russian drone has hit the headquarters of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) during a strike in the heart of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said. The unmanned aerial vehicle crashed into the SBU headquarters on Friday afternoon, targeting a room used by security chief Oleksandr Poklad. It is not clear whether Poklad was in the building, but Zelensky said he had since spoken to him to order an "appropriate, tangible response". "The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building," Zelensky confirmed. It suggests Russia's new drones are growing in accuracy and signals Moscow could step up strikes before possible US mediation talks this weekend. Trump's peace envoys to visit Moscow and Kyiv over weekend, reports say Published 9 minutes ago "All emergency services are on the scene. Everyone affected will receive the necessary assistance," Zelensky added in a message on Telegram. "I instructed Poklad to deliver an appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike, to the Russians once everything is ready. Our military will support this response." Images of the office widely shared online showed black smoke pouring from two windows on the front of the building. Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said the attack was a "major escalation that demands resolute responses". "Moscow launched this strike during a renewed push for peace - laying bare its true rejection of diplomacy," he added. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been hurt in the SBU attack, but did not elaborate on whether they were inside the offices. A nearby cafÃ© was damaged and one customer was taken to hospital after the strike. Stanislav Zavertaylo, co-owner of the popular Zavertailo chain, told the BBC that this was his third cafÃ© to have been damaged since the start of the full-scale invasion. "Now I'm in shock because there's a lot of damage. All the windows are broken, there's a lot of glass, garbage" he added. The Russian defence ministry also said on Friday it had struck a cargo vessel in the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk and a tanker near Odesa. In recent weeks Russia has escalated its daytime strikes on Ukrainian targets. In many instances it has employed jet-powered drones which are faster and harder to intercept. It is not yet known which type of munition was used in this latest attack. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Firefighters work to put out fires in the building following the Russian drone strike The strike on the SBU building is a rare example of Russia successfully hitting a government building. The SBU - which is just over the road from the St Sophia cathedral, the oldest building in Kyiv - is a key part of Ukraine's war efforts as it conducts deep strikes to damage Russian infrastructure. The drone came during yet another air raid alert. There was a brief whine before an explosion echoed across the roof tops and smoke rose into the sky. Despite the ongoing exchanges, US mediators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will visit Russia and Ukraine this weekend, reports say, as efforts to end the war continue. The envoys will meet Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday in Moscow, and then will hold talks with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday in Kyiv, Axios said, citing US officials. Witkoff and Kushner have led US President Donald Trump's efforts to broker a peace deal, without a breakthrough so far. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters View image in fullscreen People fill jerrycans with drinking water in Taiz on Wednesday. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters Yemen Besieged Yemeni city on verge of ‘unmanageable’ crisis, aid workers warn Water and fresh food running out in Taiz as fighting intensifies and Houthi advance cuts off most supply routes Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.24 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 10.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The humanitarian crisis in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz is becoming unmanageable as the city runs out of water, fuel and fresh food, Oxfam aid workers in the country have warned. Iran-allied Houthi forces have largely encircled the city of more than 900,000 people, cutting it off from most supply routes. This week, heavy fighting has raged around the city’s old airport, causing extensive damage in a densely populated residential area. The conflict has intensified since forces loyal to the internationally recognised government and the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes on the Houthi-held airport in Sana’a in July, shattering a 2022 ceasefire deal that had largely stopped the fighting. The UN has called for aid workers to be given access to Taiz. Oxfam in London called for the UK to send extra humanitarian aid to the country. The UK has allocated just £104m in aid to Yemen for each of the next three years, down from the £196m allocated in 2020. US aid to the stricken country has been virtually wiped out, and Germany, another leading funder, has halved its aid programme. Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough Read more Donor countries have subscribed to only 23% of the cost of the UN humanitarian relief programme for Yemen this year, and pressure is growing on Saudi Arabia – itself cash-strapped by the cost of war – to make up the shortfall. The World Food Programme said wheat flour reserves in the city were nearly exhausted as of mid-October. View image in fullscreen People ride past a pile of burning rubbish in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters On Tuesday the UK government allocated an unspecified sum in extra military help to Saudi Arabia to help protect its airports and infrastructure, but London has yet to decide on whether to back a much more robust military response, including supporting the possible deployment of foreign ground troops to Yemen. Fatma Jaffar, a Yemen-based advocacy manager for Oxfam, said local staff described an almost total siege of Taiz. “All the main entrances [to the city] have been blocked. The clashes are continuing and the casualties are very high,” she said. “Even people that have money are not able to buy food. Supplies are becoming very limited in the markets. No fuel has entered Taiz for two or three weeks. Drinking water is a massive issue. Even our staff are struggling to buy water. “Hospitals are struggling without medicines and a lot of people as a result are dying. Those that have been wounded by missiles – there have been attempts to get them out of the city, but because of the blockade they are not able to transfer anyone. Prices have rocketed. “Our staff told me that people are even searching for apples right now and they cannot find any fresh fruit, and basic commodities are not found inside the city. Garbage is piling up since they are not able to transfer the waste outside the city. They are trying to burn it, but we can only anticipate there will be diseases such as cholera in the near future. If this goes on much longer and access remains blocked, there will be casualties from missiles, hunger and disease from lack of water right across the city. “The situation was bad before the escalation – Yemen is one of the poorest countries on Earth – and now it is becoming unmanageable.” View image in fullscreen People wait to fill up cooking gas cylinders in Taiz. Photograph: Anees Mahyoub/Reuters Prices have rocketed: a 20-litre container of petrol that cost about $20 (£15) before the crisis is now worth $80 on the hidden market. Potato prices have doubled. The Houthi focus on Taiz reflects the city’s strategic importance, but the level of resistance inside the city may swallow the group’s resources, weakening its response elsewhere. Oxfam has been forced to transfer its limited resources from development to emergency humanitarian work, including offering cash transfers. The Halo Trust, the world’s largest humanitarian landmine-clearance organisation, said 30 of its staff were among hundreds of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city. In the Trump administration’s fiscal year 2027 budget request to Congress, the US state department has requested no economic support or development assistance specifically for Yemen. By comparison, the US committed roughly $760m in total aid to Yemen during the last year of Joe Biden’s presidency. UN diplomats are still mediating between the two sides, but there is no sign that either the Houthis or the internationally recognised government are ready for a ceasefire, let alone a long-term settlement. https://www.dw.com/en/japan-russia-ties-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OanL Journalist Yuki Imai seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on spying claims . Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept. The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia - Japan relations. Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pre-trial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release. Officials of the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been refused access to Imai. In Tokyo, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy. Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," Russia's TASS news agency reported. He has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use Japanese journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability." Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies' Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies. "One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said. "I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added. Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, said that Russia may see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for its nationals detained overseas. However, Nagy doubts Japan will give in to pressure. "They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he told DW. "It would set a dangerous precedent," he added. The arrest comes after a member of a Russia-linked hacking group "Qilin" was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center. The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released. Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024. Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court. Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance Strained Japan-Russia ties Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin . Nagy said Imai's seizure is designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East. "Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said. "This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he told DW. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo." Decades-long row over disputed islands Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Moscow, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine . Anno said Moscow's timing on turning up the heat on Tokyo is puzzling. "Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he told DW. At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II. Known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, there have been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return them to Japanese sovereignty. That campaign has faltered in the last couple of years, however, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide non-lethal assistance to Kyiv. In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands , only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands and talks are under way on the possibility of economic cooperation. https://www.politico.eu/article/leaked-e.text: BERLIN — As she was climbing the ranks of far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) a decade ago, Alice Weidel privately denounced one of her party’s most influential figures for using racist arguments and Nazi-era language, and sought to have him expelled. Years later, she praised his leadership, said a bid to ban him from the party was “exaggerated” and that he was suitable for a federal cabinet position. That striking reversal emerges from a massive leak of internal AfD communications, including emails in which Weidel condemned Björn Höcke, the party’s leader in the eastern state of Thuringia, and warned that extremists were driving away mainstream conservative voters. Advertisement Advertisement The revelations come from more than 420,000 emails and roughly 48,000 documents released by hackers this week, providing a rare glimpse inside Germany’s largest far-right party. An anonymous spokesperson for the hackers told Die Zeit the attack was not “politically” motivated “in the sense that [they] support another party,” but that they published the allegedly stolen material to promote “transparency and public accountability.” The AfD confirmed the breach, saying hackers had attacked a hosting provider in late September. It condemned the leak as “an attack on the German party system and therefore on democracy itself.” WELT, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, examined emails from one of Weidel’s accounts between 2015 and 2017, when she was a relatively junior figure in the party’s leadership. Asked by WELT to explain the contrast between her warnings at the time and her present position, Weidel declined to comment through a spokesperson. A spokesperson for Höcke did not respond to a request for comment sent by POLITICO on Saturday. ‘Deeply problematic’ The messages seen by WELT show a politician deeply alarmed by the growing influence of Höcke, who championed an ethnically defined German nationalism drawing on ideas associated with the Nazi era. Advertisement Advertisement In October 2015, Weidel warned colleagues that the party’s proximity to Pegida, an anti-Islam street movement, and the neo-Nazi National Democratic Party (now known as The Homeland) was alienating the conservative voters it needed to attract. “In the west we are losing the mainstream conservative electorate completely through our proximity to Pegida, and to the NPD in the east,” she wrote. Weidel also strongly pushed back on a speech from Höcke that same year, where he contrasted a “life-affirming African expansionary type” with a “self-negating European placeholder type,” “This is deeply problematic, because the reasoning here is racial. It is fundamentally wrong,” she wrote to the AfD’s federal executive board. “And please, spare me the usual ‘that’s-not-how-it-was-meant.’ I can’t hear it any more.” In another message, she warned that extremists were deliberately blurring the boundary between the AfD and neo-Nazi politics, driving mainstream conservatives away “in horror.” She also feared that Höcke’s rhetoric could bring the party under scrutiny by Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, its domestic intelligence service monitoring threats to the constitutional order. Advertisement Advertisement “Höcke’s statements alone, and the use of the term Volksgemeinschaft” — the Nazi-era concept of an ethnic national community — “are enough to land the AfD in that report,” she wrote, referring to the intelligence service’s annual assessment. “Some in our party seem in a hurry to drive the AfD, deliberately or not, into oblivion.” In May 2025, the agency classified the AfD as a “confirmed right-wing extremist organisation”, citing, among other things, an exclusionary concept of the German nation. The classification, which grants authorities broader surveillance powers, was provisionally suspended by a court in Cologne last February. ‘Wake up, for once’ The leak also features emails about a speech Höcke gave in January 2017 to the AfD’s youth wing, attacking Germany’s culture of Holocaust remembrance. Höcke described Berlin’s Holocaust memorial as a “memorial of shame,” criticized the country’s efforts to confront its Nazi past and demanded a “180-degree turn in the politics of memory.” Weidel herself brought a motion to expel him from the AfD. The motion, obtained by WELT, accused Höcke of using “vocabulary from Adolf Hitler” and endorsing the “ Führerprinzip ” — the Nazi doctrine of absolute leadership authority. It described him as displaying an “affinity in essence with National Socialism.” Advertisement Advertisement In an internal message, Weidel urged colleagues to recognize the implications of Höcke’s language. “Wake up, for once,” she wrote, warning of the “explosive force of the double meanings” in his speech. As Weidel prepared to seek the party’s nomination as lead candidate for the 2017 federal election, the leaked correspondence shows that she blocked the recording of her own motion against Höcke in the minutes of a party leadership meeting, arguing that further controversy would damage the party. Höcke subsequently acknowledged that his speech had been a mistake and asked the leadership to withdraw the move against him. Weidel publicly welcomed his letter as a “positive signal” and called for an end to the infighting. Within weeks, she had secured her nomination as the AfD’s lead candidate. Asked whether she would campaign alongside Höcke, she replied: “Yes, of course. We are two parts of one party.” Indeed, the emails suggest that Weidel’s private misgivings had not entirely disappeared. In May 2017, she condemned an AfD election poster featuring a pregnant woman and the slogan “‘New Germans?’ We’ll make our own” as “an NPD poster,” in a reference to the neo-Nazi party. Advertisement Advertisement Today, Weidel no longer publicly criticizes Höcke. She has praised his leadership in Thuringia and even suggested him for a federal cabinet position. “We get along very well and we got to know each other over the years,” she told BILD in a 2025 interview . When she was asked whether Höcke was suitable for a federal cabinet position, she simply replied: “Yes.” When asked in February 2025 about the 2017 expulsion proceedings against him that were backed by Weidel, Höcke called it “old news.” “We got to know each other and came to appreciate each other. Alice Weidel was the right lead candidate and did a top job,” Höcke told WELT at the time. The Axel Springer Global Reporters Network harnesses the resources of the company’s newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, The Telegraph, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms: online, print, TV and audio.
